idiom_name: Alpakka AMQP AmqpSource / AmqpSink / AmqpFlow stages
implementation_notes: Alpakka's AMQP connector expresses the adapter as stream stages: AmqpSource is an inbound adapter (a Source of IncomingMessage) and AmqpSink/AmqpFlow the outbound ones, configured by an AmqpConnectionProvider plus a list of Declarations, so the classic adapter class is replaced by graph composition and a map/mapAsync translation to application types. Choose it when an Akka/Pekko Streams runtime already exists; a blocking JMS adapter or fs2-kafka is the alternative otherwise. Prefer AmqpCachedConnectionProvider in long-running services because plain providers create a connection per materialization.
code_sketch:
val provider = AmqpCachedConnectionProvider(
  AmqpUriConnectionProvider("amqp://localhost:5672"))
val declarations = List(QueueDeclaration("orders"))

val outbound: Sink[Order, Future[Done]] =
  Flow[Order].map(o => WriteMessage(ByteString(o.toJson)))
    .to(AmqpSink.simple(AmqpSinkSettings(provider).withDeclarations(declarations)))

val inbound: Source[Order, NotUsed] =
  AmqpSource.atMostOnceSource(
    NamedQueueSourceSettings(provider, "orders"), bufferSize = 100)
    .map(m => orderFromJson(m.bytes.utf8String))
pitfalls: Connection providers materialize a new connection per stage: using AmqpUriConnectionProvider without caching silently multiplies connections, and its connection-recovery behaviour is limited.
The Source factory decides acknowledgement semantics (atMostOnceSource vs committable variants): the wrong one downgrades at-least-once to at-most-once without a compile error.
Buffer sizes on the sources/sinks are the backpressure knobs; an unbounded or oversized buffer hides a slow handler until memory runs out.
